title: 関東-九州激しい雨 夜にピークも
body:
今日26日(月)は台風から変わった低気圧が前線を伴って西日本を東進します。九州は夕方にかけて、四国や近畿は夜にかけて局地的に激しい雨が降るでしょう。東海や関東は夕方以降に雨がピークとなり、激しい雨の降る所がありそうです。大雨による土砂災害や低い土地の浸水、川の増水、道路の冠水などに注意が必要です。
台風30号は昨日25日(日)午後9時に東シナ海で温帯低気圧に変わりました。台風から変わった低気圧は前線を伴い、今日26日(月)夜にかけて九州を通って四国の南へ進むでしょう。前線の活動が活発になるため、九州から関東を中心に局地的に雨雲や雷雲が発達しそうです。
九州は昼過ぎにかけて雨のピークとなり、局地的には激しい雨や雷雨となるでしょう。夕方にかけて雨の降る所が多く、夜にはやむ見込みです。四国では断続的に雨で、特に昼前から夜遅くにかけては局地的に非常に激しい雨が降るおそれがあります。道路があっという間に冠水することが考えられますので、車の運転は注意が必要です。中国地方も雨の一日で、夕方にかけては雷を伴い雨脚の強まる所があるでしょう。近畿は昼前から夜遅くにかけて激しい雨や雷雨となる所がありそうです。帰宅時には傘を差していても濡れてしまうほどの降り方になる可能性がありますので、お気をつけください。東海や関東も次第に本降りの雨となり、夕方以降は沿岸部を中心に局地的に激しく降るでしょう。雨のピークが帰宅時間に重なりそうです。明日27日(火)の明け方にかけて大雨による土砂災害や低い土地の浸水、川の増水、道路の冠水などに注意が必要です。
激しい雨は、1時間雨量が30ミリ以上～50ミリ未満の雨を表しています。これは、バケツをひっくり返したように降るイメージです。また、傘をさしていてもぬれるレベルで、木造住宅の屋内では、寝ている人の半数くらいが雨に気づくほどです。外では道路が川のようになり、高速道路を走る車は、タイヤと路面の間に水の膜ができて、ブレーキがきかなくなる「ハイドロプレーニング現象」が起こるおそれがあります。非常に激しい雨は、1時間雨量が50ミリ以上～80ミリ未満の雨を表しています。これは、滝のように降る雨で、ゴーゴーと降り続くイメージです。また、傘は全く役にたたないレベルです。外では水しぶきで、あたり一面が白っぽくなり、視界が悪くなるため、車の運転は危険です。

title: 女性殺害 米兵関与一部ほのめかす
body:
那覇市のホテルで女性が殺害された事件で、那覇地検は25日、強盗殺人の罪で、米軍普天間飛行場（沖縄県宜野湾市）所属の海兵隊上等兵デビン・バラード容疑者（20）を起訴した。捜査関係者によると、被告は、関与を一部ほのめかす供述をしていた。当初は「私は知りません」と否認していた。【詳報】「どのような神経なのか」事件当日に歓楽街に現れた米兵　頭をそり上げ両腕にタトゥー、的中した捜査網
被告が3日の事件後、居住する基地内にいったん戻っていたことも新たに判明。再び外出し、県警が沖縄市で発見。4日に逮捕した。起訴状によると、那覇市のホテルで3日、女性の首に受話器のコードを巻き付けて殺害し、財布が入ったリュックサックを奪ったとしている。那覇地検の石井寛也次席は「公判において、法と証拠に基づき、的確な主張、立証に力を尽くしたい」とコメントした。亡くなったのは、那覇市の女性（39）。死因は窒息だった。在沖縄米軍は9日からの30日間を「反省期間」と位置付け、午前0時から同5時までの外出を禁止する対策を公表した。県議会は9日、米政府や米軍への抗議決議と日本政府への意見書を賛成多数で可決した。

title: 和菓子店主殺害 逮捕知り遺族号泣
body:
山口県で有名和菓子店の男性店主が殺害された事件で、きょう25日、20代の男2人が逮捕されました。2人の職業は害虫駆除など身の回りの困りごとに幅広く対応する、いわゆる“便利屋”業とみられています。事件現場からは、現金などの入った金庫が奪われていましたが、窓が割られたような痕跡はありませんでした。【画像】和菓子店殺人 “便利屋”業の20代男2人逮捕 遺族悲痛「頭陥没するほど殴られた」
現場の前に止まっていた1台の車。殺害された斉藤一正さんが使っていた車です。長男は、この車を手放そうとしていたとき、容疑者逮捕の知らせを受けたといいます。斉藤一正さんの長男「父のプロボックス（車）をどう使っていいのか分からなくて、下取りで、商談のさなかに（警察から）電話があって、お店の玄関先で人目もはばからず号泣してしまいました。」8月28日、山口県美祢市。地元で愛されてきた和菓子店は、この日、営業していませんでした。近くに住む長男が店を訪ねると、父親の一正さんと母親が倒れているのを発見します。80歳の一正さんは殺害され、70代の母親は大けがをしていました。2人には頭を鈍器で殴られた跡があったといいます。店の売り上げは残されていましたが、金庫は奪われていたということです。警察によると、窓が割られたり、こじ開けられたりした痕跡はなく、室内も荒らされていなかったといいます。ただ、建物の裏口のカギは開いていました。創業から約100年。3代目として店ののれんを守っていたのが、一正さんでした。斉藤一正さん「この辺は昔から石灰石は有名だから、セメントの原料の石灰石。土のついた石灰石のイメージ。見かけは悪いですけど、もっとおいしくなるように努力はしています。嫌がらずに買ってください。」
三宅晴子記者「午後6時、村岡容疑者の自宅とみられる場所に、捜査員2人が入っていきます。」事件から約2カ月。きょう、捜査が大きく動きました。村岡耕志浪容疑者26歳と、大倉万輝容疑者27歳が、強盗殺人の疑いなどで逮捕されました。村岡容疑者は山口県周南市、大倉容疑者は広島市に住んでいて、現場の美祢市とは、それほど近いわけではありません。2人に共通していたのが、仕事です。警察によると、村岡容疑者は便利業を営み、大倉容疑者も、自称、便利業をしていると話しているということです。便利業は、いわゆる“便利屋”として仕事を請け負っています。害虫駆除やカギを紛失した際の開錠、エアコンの清掃など、室内に入る場面も多くあります。事件との関連は分かりませんが、現場では裏口のカギが開いていました。一部の部屋に物色された痕跡はあったものの、無差別に荒らされた様子はなかったといいます。警察によると、2人は防犯カメラなどの捜査で浮上。現時点で、一正さんの親族や知人ではなく、関係のない他人だとしています。周南市で暮らしていた村岡容疑者。近隣住民によると、自身の子どもを含めた4世代で暮らしていたといいます。近隣住民「あそこの家に詳しい人はいないです。この近所であそこの家と仲がいいという方はいない。（登校時など朝の）旗当番でも全然時間になっても来ないことがあったので。子どもたちだけで勝手にいくとかそういうことがよくあった。」村岡容疑者と大倉容疑者は知人だったとみられています。

title: チャイルドシートの義務拡大 検討
body:
重大な交通事故から子供の命を守るため、警察庁はチャイルドシート（ジュニアシートを含む）を使用する基準の拡大に向け、本格的な検討に入った。道路交通法で６歳未満の「幼児」としている着用義務の範囲を広げ、身長が低い１３歳未満の児童らも対象とすることが想定される。【イラスト解説】チャイルドシート基準、こう変わる
要件の見直しには道交法の改正が必要となる。同庁は近く、交通工学に詳しい大学教授や、医師らで構成する有識者検討会を設置する方針だ。
６歳以上でも身長が低い児童がシートベルトを着用すると、胸骨や腰骨といった正しい位置にベルトがかからず、事故の衝撃を受けた際に、首や腹部に食い込んで危険なことがある。
福岡市早良区で２０２４年８月に軽乗用車と路線バスが衝突した事故では、軽乗用車側の当時７歳と５歳の女児２人が、腹部付近にかかったシートベルトに腹部を圧迫されるなどして死亡につながった。
事故当時、日本自動車連盟（ＪＡＦ）ではチャイルドシートの使用が推奨される子供の身長の目安を「１メートル４０未満」と周知していた。２人は身長１メートル４０未満だったが、いずれもチャイルドシートやジュニアシートは使用していなかった。
ＪＡＦは事故後の２４年９月、推奨される身長を「１メートル５０未満」に引き上げた。警察庁も、シートベルトを適切に着用できない児童については、６歳以上でもチャイルドシートを使用するよう注意喚起してきたが、国会では「基準の拡大が必要」との指摘が出ていた。
チャイルドシートは、適正に使用すれば、死亡のリスクを下げる効果がある。同庁が昨年までの過去５年間に発生した幼児が同乗する車の事故を分析した結果、チャイルドシートを使用していなかった幼児の致死率は、適正に使用していた幼児の約５倍に上った。

title: コニカミノルタ「社内副業」狙い
body:
電機・光学メーカーのコニカミノルタ（東京都千代田区）は7月、高度な専門スキルを持つ人材を事業横断で活用する「スキルシェア制度」（社内副業）を導入し、SNSを中心に話題を集めた。【画像】本業の成果をきちんと出した上で、社内副業に取り組む1案件当たり最大月20時間、最長3カ月にわたり、社員が現在の部署に所属したまま、他部門で“社内副業”という形で働ける仕組みだ。業務時間に応じた追加手当も支給する。2025年から実施した2回のトライアルでは、36件の業務依頼のうち27件で、担当する社員とのマッチングが成立。外部委託費の抑制や、これまで手が回らなかった業務の推進といった効果も確認できたという。スキルシェア制度の仕組みや導入の背景、今後の展開について、コニカミノルタで人事部 技術人財強化グループリーダー（部長）を務める大西和子氏に聞いた。
スキルシェア制度は、社員が現在の部署に所属したまま、専門スキルを生かして他部門の業務に取り組む仕組みだ。人材育成を主な目的とするインターンシップとは異なり、専門性を生かして実際に業務上の成果を出すことを重視している。一般的な兼務の仕組みでは、本業の勤務時間の一部を別部門の業務に充てる方法もある。一方、コニカミノルタのスキルシェア制度は、本業の時間は削らず、通常業務の成果や品質も維持することが前提だ。その上で、専門性を生かした追加業務に取り組むとしている。業務時間は月5時間、10時間、20時間の3つの枠を設け、期間は最長3カ月とする。募集する部門が、案件の内容や必要な支援の量に応じて設定する。例えば、スキルを持つ人の知見を聞きたい程度なら月5時間、一定の作業を伴う案件なら月10時間や20時間と、必要に応じて使い分けられる。スキルシェア制度に参加した社員には、通常の給与とは別に、業務時間に応じた手当を支給する。月20時間の案件なら10万円、10時間なら5万円、5時間なら2万5000円だ。手当は人事部ではなく、業務を依頼する部門が負担する。手当は、社員の年齢や給与グレードにかかわらず、業務時間に応じて一律に支給する。20時間で10万円という金額は、一般社員の中で最も高い給与グレードの時間単価を基準に設定した。「専門性を要する業務ができるかどうかで募集しているので、社員のグレードにかかわらず同じ基準で手当を支給すべきだと考えた。ITスキルやデータサイエンスの領域は、必ずしも中堅社員が若手より長けているとは限らない。若手社員が手を挙げてやってくれることもある」（大西氏）制度の導入に合わせ、社員と業務をマッチングするプラットフォームも内製で開発した。マッチング方法は、事業部門が提示した業務に社員が応募する「募集型」と、登録されたプロフィールを基に、依頼する部門が特定の社員に声をかける「指名型」の2種類だ。応募の際は、現職の上司の許可が必要だ。応募後は書類選考や面接を行い、依頼部門、参加社員、現職の上司の3者で業務内容などを確認し、合意した上で開始する。トライアル段階では、上司の承認を得るタイミングを後の段階に設定していたため、部下が他部門の業務に参加することによる本業への影響を懸念する声も上がった。本格導入では、応募前に上司の承認を得る運用に変更した。

title: 金正恩氏の訪中 習氏とは会談せず
body:
【丹東共同】北朝鮮の金正恩朝鮮労働党総書記は24日に国境沿いの中国遼寧省丹東を訪れ、中国共産党序列4位の王滬寧・人民政治協商会議（政協）主席と会談した一方、習近平国家主席とは会わなかった。昨年9月までの過去5回の訪中ではいずれも習氏と会談しており、首脳間で接触がなかったのは初めて。【画像】中国軍「もし戦争が今日勃発したら、これが答えだ」「開戦動画」で威嚇
北朝鮮の最高指導者が外遊で相手国の首脳級と会わないのは異例。今回の訪中は日帰りで、中国側の重要会議である第20期中央委員会第5回総会（5中総会）の直前だったことが日程調整に影響したとみられる。25日の北朝鮮メディアの報道によると、金氏は王氏との会談で「われわれの訪問に特別でこまやかな気配りをしてくれた習氏に感謝する」と述べた。

title: オバマ氏 トランプ政権を痛烈批判
body: 【AFP＝時事】バラク・オバマ米元大統領（65）は24日、11月3日の中間選挙の民主党候補を応援するためにオハイオ州クリーブランドで開かれた集会に参加し、ドナルド・トランプ大統領を痛烈に批判した。【写真】クリーブランドの集会に応援に駆け付けたオバマ米元大統領、他オバマ氏は、「現代では前例のない混乱と残酷さ、腐敗、無能さが2年間続いている。『もうたくさんだ』と言う機会だ」と述べ、「ここオハイオ州で、私たちは変化を求めて投票する」と訴えた。オバマ氏は、燃料価格の高騰を背景に、有権者の大きな懸念事項の一つとなっている生活費の上昇について、トランプ政権に責任があると非難。「現職大統領は一連の誤った決断を下した。中でも最も重大なのは、誰も望んでいない不必要な戦争を始める決断をしたことだ」と指摘した。また、同州ではすでに期日前投票が始まっているとして、有権者にできるだけ早く投票するよう呼びかけ、「先延ばしにせず、ためらわずに」と訴えた。オバマ氏は今も民主党支持層の間で高い人気を誇っており、連邦議会の主導権を左右する重要な中間選挙で、党の候補者を支援するために自身の人気を生かそうとしている。オハイオ州では、民主党のシェロッド・ブラウン元上院議員が共和党の現職ジョン・ハステッド上院議員を相手に返り咲きを目指す。一方、州知事選では、民主党のエイミー・アクトン氏と、2024年の大統領選で共和党の候補者指名を争ったビベック・ラマスワミ氏が対決する。同州の世論調査では、いずれの選挙戦でも民主党候補がわずかにリードしているが、接戦になると予想されている。全米の世論調査でも、民主党が下院の主導権を奪還する可能性が示されており、上院でも厳しい接戦が予想されている。オバマ氏はクリーブランドでの集会後、同日夜にはミシガン州に移動し、デトロイトで民主党の上院議員候補アブドゥル・エルサイード氏と共に集会に参加する予定だ。ミシガン州の上院議員2議席は現在、いずれも民主党が占めているが、党内左派のエルサイード氏は共和党のマイク・ロジャース氏と接戦を繰り広げている。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: フランス全土でデモ再び 厳戒態勢
body: フランス各地で24日、生活苦や公共サービスへの不満を理由とする大規模なデモが行われた。17日のデモには事前予測を上回る計55万人（内務省発表）が参加し、一部で暴動や略奪も発生したことから、当局は全国で7万人の警察官らを配置する厳戒態勢を敷いた。【写真】マクロン大統領=AP。｢暴動は、マクロン氏の路線が招いた帰結だ｣と東大の中山洋平教授は指摘する24日、パリで労働組合などが参加するデモの出発地点には、開始前から数百人が集結。若者らが「マクロン（大統領）辞めろ」と叫んだ。医療や教育などの公共サービスへの不満を記したメッセージボードも見られた。パリのデモに参加した大学生のアナイス・ルゲネックさん（20）は「マクロン政権は国民の声を聞いていない。ケアが必要な人、生活に苦しんでいる人が無視されている」と憤る。自身は恵まれていると話しつつ、インフレ（物価高）の影響は日々感じる。「食べる量を減らすようにした」。マクロン政権は、そうした一般市民の苦しみを十分に認識していないと感じるという。パリのレピュブリック広場では、1週間前の騒乱の爪痕がなお残り、焼け落ちた露店やひび割れたガラスがそのままになっていた。付近の店は板で外壁を補強し、貼り紙で一時休業を知らせる店舗も目立つ。■デモの制限、｢もはやフランスではない｣現地メディアによると、当局はパリで労組が申請したデモ行進のルートを認めず、中心部から離れたルートに変更した。中部リヨンでは集会の禁止区域に集まったとして、治安当局が催涙弾を使って人々を解散させたという。マクロン大統領は22日、労組以外のデモは原則として禁じると表明。都市中心部での活動も認めない方針だ。AFP通信によると、24日は全国で前週より2割多い警備要員を投入。ルーブル美術館も安全のため閉鎖された。ただ、デモの制限や警察の対応には批判が相次いでおり、フランスの環境政党のトンドリエ党首は23日、デモをする自由さえ損なわれたとして、「もう自分の国だと思えない」とラジオ番組で批判。人権擁護などに取り組む国際機関「欧州評議会」のマイケル・オフラハティ人権弁務官も23日、欧州各地で週末にデモが行われることを踏まえ、「平和的に集会する権利を保障し、警察活動が人権に適合した形で行われる」ことを求めた。フランス内務省によると、17日の騒乱に際しては、2397人が拘束され、警察官と憲兵計997人が負傷した。商業施設の被害も甚大で、政府は17、18日に「数千店」が被害を受けたと発表している。（パリ=藤原学思）

title: 平和賞マチャド氏 ベネズエラ帰国
body: Vivian Sequera　Sarah Kinosian　Keren Torres[カラカス／バルキシメト ２５日 ロイター] - ベネズエラの野党指導者でノーベル平和賞受賞者のマリア・コリナ・マチャド氏が２５日、約１年ぶりに帰国した。これ‌まで何度か帰国を試みたものの実現していなかった。マチャド氏はＸに「私⁠はここにいる。皆さんと共に」と投稿した。広報担当者が公開した画像によると、同氏は西部ララ州の教会に姿を見せた。ロイター記者によれば、居合わせ​た人々は国歌を歌って出迎え、同氏が車で去る際には「自由を」と叫んだ。陸路で首都カラカスに向かうという。帰国に向けた取り組みはトラ‌ンプ政権との関係を試すものとなった。マチャド氏は米政権が１月にマドゥロ大統領を拘束する以前から、同政権を味方に引き入れようと関係構築に努めていた。ロ‌イターが６月に報じたところによると、‌米政府はマチャド氏に帰国を遅らせるよう少なくとも１回要請​しており、同氏はこれまで何度か入国を試みたものの実現しなかった。同氏のチームは今回、どの‌ように帰国したか詳細を明らかにしていない。トランプ氏は、マドゥロ氏の下で副大統領を務めたロドリゲス暫定大統‌領への支持を繰り返し表明。米企業​によるベネズエラでの石油生産や他の事業に関する合意を称賛‌してきた。９月には、同国で民主的な選挙を検討するのは時期尚早だと述べた。トランプ氏は２５日、ホワイトハウスで、マ⁠チャド氏の帰国については何も知らないと述べ、米国が引き続きロドリゲス氏を支持することを示唆した。マチャド氏について「彼女はとても素敵な女性だ」としつつ、「だが、われわれはベネズエラ⁠で非常にうまくやっている」と語った。事情に詳しい関係​者２人によると、マチャド氏は‌パナマからプライベート機でコロンビアに移動し、その後、陸路でベネズエラに入った。ルビオ米国務長官は声明で「マチャド氏の安全な帰国を可能にした環境は、米国が支援する⁠和解協議の直接的な成果だ。この協議によって既に数百人の政治犯が釈放さ⁠れ、亡命していた野党関係者数百人が帰国した」と表明。「全ての政治勢力がこの協議を支持する⁠ことを期待する。ベネズエラにとって、自由で公正な選挙だけでなく、持続的な民主主義を平和的に実現す‌る上で、⁠過去３０年間で最良の機会だ」と述べた。マチャド氏はマドゥロ政権によって出国を禁じ​られていたが、１年以上にわたりほぼ身を隠して生活した後、ノーベル平和賞授賞式に合わせて２０２５年末に秘密裏に出国していた。

title: NY大司教区 性的虐待で和解合意
body: 【AFP＝時事】米ニューヨーク大司教区は24日、聖職者による性的虐待の被害者らに8億ドル（約1255億円）超を支払うことで和解に合意したと発表した。【写真】教皇候補にも名を挙げられた枢機卿、複数の女性から性的暴行で告発される和解合意書は11月上旬に正式に署名される予定で、原告側の弁護士との長年にわたる交渉が決着する。米紙ニューヨーク・タイムズによると、被害者約1300人にそれぞれ少なくとも25万ドルが支払われる。虐待の深刻さに応じ、支払額がさらに増える可能性もある。米国のカトリック教会では、2000年代初頭から性的虐待をめぐる不祥事が相次いでいる。ニューヨーク大司教のロナルド・ヒックス氏は、司祭らに送ったメールで「神のお導きにより、被害を受けたすべての人々に少しでも癒やしと和解をもたらすことができるところまで来ている」と述べた。大司教区がメールをAFPに転送した。ヒックス氏は昨年、ローマ・カトリック教会の教皇レオ14世により、影響力のある保守派のティモシー・ドーラン枢機卿の後任としてニューヨーク大司教に任命された。ドーラン氏は退任前、性的虐待の被害者への補償に充てる基金の設立を発表していた。2000年代には、報道機関の調査により、米国のカトリック司祭が数十年にわたり数千人の子どもに性的虐待を加えていたことが明らかになった。教会指導者らが事件を隠蔽（いんぺい）したり、加害者の司祭を捜査当局に通報せずに異動させたりしていた事例も多く判明した。全米各地の教区は数億ドル規模の損害賠償の支払いを余儀なくされ、裁判を経ずに被害者に補償する制度も設けられている。【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: AI投資に巨額マネー 実態と展望
body:
米大手IT企業の債券発行額が過去最高水準に達し、データセンターや計算資源に対する巨額の設備投資が過熱している。その一方で、生成AI開発企業による巨額の損失計上や、AI関連企業の抱える負債の急増など、先行投資の回収可能性に対する市場の警戒感も急速に高まっている。【映像】AIへの多額投資、識者たちの見解天文学的な資金が流れ込むAIビジネスは、社会に劇的な変革をもたらす産業革命となるのか、それとも持続不能なバブル崩壊の引き金となるのか。テクノロジー投資の実態と今後の展望について、『ABEMA Prime』で議論が行われた。
番組ではまず、AI市場に注ぎ込まれるマネーの急膨張と、それに伴う財務リスクの現状が紹介された。米AI開発企業「アンソロピック」が今年上半期で約12兆7000億円（807億ドル）もの純損失を計上、このうち約720億ドルは転換社債などの評価変動に伴う会計上の費用だった。大手IT企業5社（アマゾン、メタ、マイクロソフトなど）の債券発行額の合計も前年の約17兆円から倍増し、過去最高の約35兆円（2187億ドル）に達している事実が示された。近畿大学情報学研究所所長・夏野剛氏は、現在のAI開発競争における資金調達構造の特徴について、「AIのビジネスモデルが全く確立していない中で今何が起こっているかといえば、Googleは手元資金でやっている。それに対してOpenAIやアンソロピックは外部調達でやっている。ビジネスモデルができていない状況で、2つの全く異なる資金調達方法で競争しているというのは史上初めてのことだ」と解説した。さらに夏野氏は、「ここで例えばOpenAIやアンソロピックに何かあったら大クラッシュが起こるが、Googleだけは影響を受けない。AI全体の進化そのものにはあまり影響はないが、経済的、市場的にはものすごいクラッシュが起こる可能性がある」と指摘した。

title: 10月FOMCは金利据え置きか 焦点
body: ■要旨・米国10月FOMCでは政策金利据え置きの見通しが濃厚である。・高止まりするインフレとAI設備投資の持続性を巡る評価が焦点。・米FRBウォーシュ議長の会見や改革提言の進捗にも注目である。【写真を見る】10月FOMCは金利据え置きか インフレ認識とAI投資の持続性を探る■据え置きが見込まれる10月FOMC2026年10月FOMC（10/27〜28催）において、FRBは賛成多数で政策金利（3.75〜4.00％）を据え置く可能性が高い。FRBは9月FOMCにて米国経済の堅調な推移やインフレ高止まりを踏まえ、23年7月以来となる0.25％の利上げに踏み切った。また、同時に公表されたドットチャートで年内に追加で1回の利上げ見通しが示された。8月CPI及びFRBのタカ派的なスタンスを踏まえて、金融市場は連続利上げの可能性を徐々に織り込んでいったものの、FRB高官は9月末から10月初めにかけてこれに慎重なスタンスを示した。例えば、9/29にウィリアムズ総裁は「急ぐ必要はなく、情報を集める時間がある」、10/1にジェファーソン副議長は「（政策判断には）もう少し時間がかかるかもしれない」とそれぞれ述べた。この結果、本稿執筆時点におけるFF金利先物市場（Fed Watch）において、83.9％の確率で金利据え置きが見込まれる一方、0.25％ptの利上げ予想は16.1％に留まる。なお、金融市場は12月FOMCにおける0.25％の利上げに加えて、2027年末に向けて更に2回程度の利上げを織り込んでいる。この場合の合計利上げ幅は+1.0％ptとなり、9月時点のドットチャート（26年に計0.5％ptの利上げを行い、27年は据え置き）を上回る。もっとも、過去の利上げ局面ではそれが1〜2回に留まることは稀であり、金融市場はこうした過去の事例も一部に織り込んでいるとみられる。10月地区連銀経済報告（10/14公表;10/5までの情報に基づく）では「経済活動は12地区中9地区で小幅から緩やかに拡大した（2地区がmoderate growth、3地区がmodest growth、4地区がslight growth）」とまとめられた。また、「労働市場は総じて変化がなかった」と指摘した。一方、「物価上昇は3地区で力強く上昇し、8地区で緩やかに上昇した。8地区のうち3地区では投入価格の上昇圧力が強まっている」とインフレ高止まりへの懸念が強調された。また、複数の地区でインフレによる生活費負担の増大が賃金の上昇圧力になっている可能性が指摘された。10月FOMCまでには10/27に9月耐久財受注や10月コンファレンスボード消費者信頼感指数などが公表されるものの、10月FOMCの政策判断に大きな影響を与える可能性は低い。

title: コニカミノルタ「社内副業」狙い
body:
電機・光学メーカーのコニカミノルタ（東京都千代田区）は7月、高度な専門スキルを持つ人材を事業横断で活用する「スキルシェア制度」（社内副業）を導入し、SNSを中心に話題を集めた。【画像】本業の成果をきちんと出した上で、社内副業に取り組む1案件当たり最大月20時間、最長3カ月にわたり、社員が現在の部署に所属したまま、他部門で“社内副業”という形で働ける仕組みだ。業務時間に応じた追加手当も支給する。2025年から実施した2回のトライアルでは、36件の業務依頼のうち27件で、担当する社員とのマッチングが成立。外部委託費の抑制や、これまで手が回らなかった業務の推進といった効果も確認できたという。スキルシェア制度の仕組みや導入の背景、今後の展開について、コニカミノルタで人事部 技術人財強化グループリーダー（部長）を務める大西和子氏に聞いた。
スキルシェア制度は、社員が現在の部署に所属したまま、専門スキルを生かして他部門の業務に取り組む仕組みだ。人材育成を主な目的とするインターンシップとは異なり、専門性を生かして実際に業務上の成果を出すことを重視している。一般的な兼務の仕組みでは、本業の勤務時間の一部を別部門の業務に充てる方法もある。一方、コニカミノルタのスキルシェア制度は、本業の時間は削らず、通常業務の成果や品質も維持することが前提だ。その上で、専門性を生かした追加業務に取り組むとしている。業務時間は月5時間、10時間、20時間の3つの枠を設け、期間は最長3カ月とする。募集する部門が、案件の内容や必要な支援の量に応じて設定する。例えば、スキルを持つ人の知見を聞きたい程度なら月5時間、一定の作業を伴う案件なら月10時間や20時間と、必要に応じて使い分けられる。スキルシェア制度に参加した社員には、通常の給与とは別に、業務時間に応じた手当を支給する。月20時間の案件なら10万円、10時間なら5万円、5時間なら2万5000円だ。手当は人事部ではなく、業務を依頼する部門が負担する。手当は、社員の年齢や給与グレードにかかわらず、業務時間に応じて一律に支給する。20時間で10万円という金額は、一般社員の中で最も高い給与グレードの時間単価を基準に設定した。「専門性を要する業務ができるかどうかで募集しているので、社員のグレードにかかわらず同じ基準で手当を支給すべきだと考えた。ITスキルやデータサイエンスの領域は、必ずしも中堅社員が若手より長けているとは限らない。若手社員が手を挙げてやってくれることもある」（大西氏）制度の導入に合わせ、社員と業務をマッチングするプラットフォームも内製で開発した。マッチング方法は、事業部門が提示した業務に社員が応募する「募集型」と、登録されたプロフィールを基に、依頼する部門が特定の社員に声をかける「指名型」の2種類だ。応募の際は、現職の上司の許可が必要だ。応募後は書類選考や面接を行い、依頼部門、参加社員、現職の上司の3者で業務内容などを確認し、合意した上で開始する。トライアル段階では、上司の承認を得るタイミングを後の段階に設定していたため、部下が他部門の業務に参加することによる本業への影響を懸念する声も上がった。本格導入では、応募前に上司の承認を得る運用に変更した。

title: Suicaペンギンなぜ「卒業」解説
body: 誕生から25年。移動の顔として定着したあのキャラクターが、“卒業”まで半年を切った。■【画像】Suicaペンギンのもととなった絵本「JR東日本は、2027年3月31日をもってSuicaのペンギンを卒業させます。ペンギンが描かれた現行のSuicaカードも、在庫がなくなり次第、販売を終了。その後は、キャラクターのいない無地のカードに切り替わる予定です」（全国紙社会部記者）Suicaの顔は2027年4月1日に新たなイメージキャラクターに交代する予定だ。そのペンギンの卒業をめぐっては、一企業のキャラクターとしては異例の盛り上がりを見せている。「10月1日から全30か所を巡るデジタルスタンプラリーがスタート。東京駅では10月21日まで『SuicaのペンギンフェアFINAL』が開催され、新作10商品を含む24商品が並びました。このほかにも、限定グッズやポイントが当たるキャンペーンも始まっています」（前同）JR東日本は、ペンギン卒業の理由として、Suicaを従来の「移動と少額決済のデバイス」から、日々の暮らし全体を支える「生活のデバイス」へ進化させるためだと説明しているが、それでもSuicaと言えばペンギンのイメージは根強い。その人気は凄まじく、卒業撤回を求めるオンライン署名が2万6000人超も集まったほどだ。これほどの人気者なら、企業にとっても大きな“資産”のはず──。それなのに、なぜJR東日本はその資産を手放すのか。キャラクタービジネスに詳しいキャラクター・データバンク社長の陸川和男氏は、企業戦略としては珍しいことではないと話す。「企業キャラクターは、あくまでサービスの訴求やブランディングのためのもの。商品化のために作られたキャラクターとは分けて考えないといけません。例えば『ドコモダケ』は、ドコモのサービスを訴求するために作られたキャラクターでした。そのサービスがある程度浸透したら使われなくなり、また最近になって復活しています。サービスの転換に合わせてキャラクターを変えることは、企業論理としてはそれほど珍しくありません」ただ、Suicaのペンギンは、一企業のキャラクターの域を超えているのは前述の通りだ。「Suicaのペンギンは、あまりに浸透して人気があり、ファンもたくさんいる。一般的な企業キャラクターとは少し違う立ち位置になっています。撤回を求める声まで出るのは、異例中の異例でしょうね。ここまでの反響は、JR東日本にとっても予想外だった可能性があります」（前同）

title: 美容室の倒産高水準 競争で二極化
body:
店舗数が全国で27万店以上と言われる美容室の倒産が高止まりしている。2026年度上半期（4-9月）の「美容業」倒産は54件（前年同期比6.8％減）で、年度上半期では4年ぶりに前年を下回った。ただ、2年連続の50件台で、2007年度以降の20年間では、前年（58件）に次ぐ2番目の高水準だった。負債総額は20億5,100万円（同2.4％増）で、2年連続で増加した。負債1億円未満が51件（同1.9％減）で全体の94.4％（前年同期89.6％）を占め、過小資本の美容室の淘汰が進んでいる。美容室は、比較的少ない資金で開業でき、新規参入が相次ぎ、生存競争が激しい業界になっている。低価格店舗もジワリと広がるなか、人気の美容師やデザイン力などで固定客の確保を進め、ブランド力と高付加価値の創出で差別化を図れるかが問われている。原因別では、最多は販売不振が41件（前年同期比12.7％減）で、全体の75.9％を占めた。資本金別は、1千万円未満が48件（前年同期比12.7％減、構成比88.8％）で、うち個人企業他が22件（同12.0％減、同40.7％）と小・零細規模が多いことが特徴だ。こうした資産背景に乏しい小・零細規模の美容室は、顧客に応じた接客や施術力のほか、SNSのフォロワー増加などで集客力を強化し、差別化を図れないと生き残りが難しいことを示している。「人手不足」倒産は5件（前年同期比150.0％増、前年同期2件）で、2021年度同期の4件を超え過去最多を更新した。美容師の人手不足が続くなか、小・零細規模の美容室は、美容師自体のブランド力や差別化も求められている。安定顧客を獲得できない美容室の淘汰は続きそうだ。※本調査は、日本産業分類（細分類）の「美容業」を抽出し、2007年度から2026年度までの上半期倒産を集計、分析した。
✔原因別：販売不振が41件（前年同期比12.7％減、構成比75.9％）で最多。次いで、既往のシワ寄せが4件（同100.0％増、同7.4％）、他社倒産の余波（前年同期同数）、運転資金の欠乏（前年同期同数）がそれぞれ3件。✔資本金別：個人企業他が22件（前年同期比12.0％減、構成比40.7％）で最多。以下、1百万円以上5百万円未満が21件（同31.2％増、同38.8％）、1千万円以上5千万円未満が6件（同200.0％増、同11.1％）、5百万円以上1千万円未満が4件（同33.3％減、同7.4％）。✔負債額別：最多は1千万円以上5千万円未満が39件（前年同期比20.4％減、構成比72.2％）で、以下、5千万円以上1億円未満が12件（同300.0％増、同22.2％）。

title: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
summary: The populist right-wing leader of 12 years says it is "clear" his party has lost the vote billed as a referendum on the country's future.
body:
Watch: Joy and disbelief on Serbian streets as Vučić concedes election defeat
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to the student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.
"We still do not have final results... it is clear that we have lost these elections," the right-wing populist leader said as he conceded late on Sunday.
Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission indicated a record high turnout, which commentators had suggested would favour the student movement.
Vučić had called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.
Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost
Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."
He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".
Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.
There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.  "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."
The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told the BBC Serbian.
The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.
Ilija Srdanović, Student List's leading candidate, pictured during celebrations late on Sunday
The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.
Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.
Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close.
Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.
This was also the case outside booths in number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.
In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.
The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.

title: Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election
summary: After three years of regional war, this is a battle Israel always knew was coming, writes Lucy Williamson.
body:
Watch: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history
After three years of regional war, this is a battle Israel always knew was coming.
The general election on Tuesday hangs over a country that's deeply divided and ready for a fight.
Polls published on Friday put the governing coalition and the main opposition bloc almost neck-and-neck, with half a million first-time voters due to cast their ballot and some 70,000 Israelis reportedly flying in from abroad specifically to vote.
On Saturday night, vast crowds of opposition voters gathered in central Tel Aviv to demand a change of government.
"We're optimistic," 21-year-old Omri told me. "I want peace, I want security, and I want to end corruption and get the religious fanatics out."
This campaign has been energized by new tactics - including AI videos designed to grab the headlines - and also by a new face.
Gadi Eisenkot is, perhaps, not the man you might expect to take on the flashy, aggressive, media-savvy brand of Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?
Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters
The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
Relatively new to politics, with a working-class Moroccan background, Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff who is renowned for his calm manner and low-drama approach. He's been dubbed by some as a "non-politician".
But he and his centrist Yashar party have regularly pipped Netanyahu and his Likud party to the top spot in recent polls, the last of which was published on Friday, in line with Israeli election law.
Israeli politics is the art of coalition-building, rather than the task of any one party winning power, but with the predicted result too close to call, Eisenkot's rising profile has sharpened a race many Israelis already see as existential for the future of their country.
I watched him slip past the cameras at a community centre for Ethiopian Jews in the city of Ramle last week, through a gaggle of security personnel and advisors.
One of those who had come to hear him speak was David, a smartly dressed man in a freshly-pressed shirt and navy jacket, who said he had met Eisenkot before.
"He looks you in the eye, not like a leader looking down at someone," David told me. "And he listens. He's very sympathetic."
Eisenkot's image as a "non-politician" has proved popular
Eisenkot's appeal is often put down to his personal manner and profile. A softly-spoken military man whose son was killed during the Gaza War, he has presented himself as coming "from the periphery", not from Israel's wealthy urban elite.
His Moroccan background became election headlines earlier this month when a pro-Netanyahu speaker used a racist slur to refer to Eisenkot during a TV debate, referring to him as a Moroccan "monkey".
"These elections are about many issues," Eisenkot told the crowd gathered at the Ramle community centre. "They are about security, economy, education...but primarily, they are about the identity of the State of Israel, and what kind of Israel we want to see. A Jewish state, a democratic state, a liberal, tolerant, egalitarian state."
This is music to opposition ears, who say Benjamin Netanyahu's government is a threat to Israel's democracy, pointing to his efforts to curb the powers of the judicial system, and his refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks on the grounds that the country's Supreme Court would be biased against him.
Eisenkot, along with other opposition leaders, has attempted to draw voters away from Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party by promising such a state inquiry, which a recent survey suggests is supported by more than 70% of Jewish Israelis.
Protesters gathered in Tel Aviv on Saturday to demand a state commission of enquiry into the October 7 attacks
He has also vowed to enforce court rulings on drafting ultra-Orthodox Jews into national military service - another measure that is popular with right-wing voters and opposition alike.
Benjamin Netanyahu has hit back with a campaign focused on Israel's security, and a core campaign slogan of "No Surrender".
He has repeatedly cast his rivals as soft on security, playing on the fears of some right-wing voters that Jewish opposition parties might ally with Israel's Arab parties to secure a majority, and suggesting this could compromise national security.
Around one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.
These are the first elections since the 7 October attacks, in which Hamas-led gunmen stormed through Gaza's border fence, killing almost people and taking 251 hostage.
It was Israel's worst security failure, but three years on its prime minister is again running for re-election as the only man who can keep Israel safe.
"If the army had woken him in time, it wouldn't have happened," Shlomi Bashar told me, one of several die-hard Netanyahu fans drinking in a basement café in Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda market. "He does bear a certain responsibility, but after the 7 October, he changed the entire Middle East."
Netanyahu has been hammering home the message that Israel's wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, in the years after the 7 October attacks, have reduced existential threats to the country.
"We need him to be re-elected so that he can finish this work," said Shlomi. "In my opinion, he is one of the best leaders in the world. Most of the world loves him and respects him, because he is a strong man and his ideas are correct."
Shlomi Bashar is a long-time Netanyahu supporter
The prime minister has traditionally relied on a stable base of right-wing voters, but is projected to see a thinning of support in this election. Some voters may be slipping away to opposition parties like Eisenkot's. Others, including some die-hard Likud voters we spoke to, said the 7 October attacks had pushed them towards parties further on the right.
Lt Col (Res) Eyal Hajbi, head of the regional civil defence unit in the Netanyahu stronghold of Sderot, right on the Gaza border, lost several friends and colleagues in the attacks. He lights candles for them every day in his office, and told me he would be thinking about them when he cast his ballot on Tuesday.
Standing on a ridge overlooking the ruins of northern Gaza, he gestured to the wasteland where Israel's army has completely flattened the neighbourhoods of Beit Lahia and Beit Hanoun.
"As far as I'm concerned, after 7 October, we should wipe them all out," he said. "I've changed my understanding of Gaza. Before, I wouldn't have said we should destroy it."
He told me he and his family had always voted Likud, but that now he was voting for the far-right party of Itamar Ben Gvir, Jewish Power.
"My family has become more extreme than it ever was before," he said. "If once we deliberated over it, today we don't think twice; we vote."
Polls suggest that less than 10% of Israelis are undecided and that very few of those are considering switching between government parties and opposition ones.
Ben Gvir, National Security minister in Netanyahu's coalition, has been reaching out to younger voters through headline-grabbing social media campaigns.
A poll for one of Israel's leading newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth, published on 9 October, suggested that more than 16% of first-time voters in Israel would choose far-right parties like his.
In Sderot, a group of 18 year olds from a nearby Jewish religious college told me their political views had been affected by the 7 October attacks far more than their parents. All four teenagers were planning to vote for another far-right party, Religious Zionism, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
"Today, the whole younger generation understands that peaceful paths will not work," Aviad Elmahach, one of the teenagers, told me. "Older adults, who are set in a fixed mindset, find [it] harder to change, but the youth understand that we need to be here with strength and an iron fist, which is the only way to win."
The lesson of 7 October, he said, was that Israel needed to be as forceful as possible in its relations with the Palestinians, more than 74,000 of whom have been killed by Israel in Gaza since then, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
"The youth have a fresh new perspective that has not yet become entrenched in politics, and they understand very well why we're voting for Smotrich - it means holding the land with strength and giving [the Palestinians] nothing through peaceful gestures."
Israel's military campaign in Gaza has left much of the territory in ruins
A little further south along the Gaza border are the kibbutzim that were overrun by gunmen during the Hamas attacks. They were renowned for decades as bastions of the Israeli left.
Among them is Nir Oz, where 47 people were killed and 76 taken hostage that day.
Three years on, residents are moving back. Twenty-six-year-old Gal Pauker has opened a Friday wine café at the edge of his small vineyard next to the Gaza border - a few wooden tables set out under sheets of beige canvas to shade customers from the strong desert sun. His grandfather Gideon was killed during the 7 October attacks.
I asked Gal, and his mother Galia, whether the those attacks had shifted their political views.
Nir Oz was one of the worst hit kibbutzim on 7 October
"We need a change - we can't live with this government anymore," Galia said. "And I'm not talking about security, I'm talking first about humanity."
Having voted for centrist parties in the past, Galia says she's decided to vote for Eisenkot this time around, because "he's an ordinary guy and I hope he'll continue the way he's talking".

title: Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
summary: Machado had left the country just a month before the US government seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
body:
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile.
"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.
In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro.
The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.
Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands.
She then began travelling to the capital Caracas in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters have lined the route of her journey to the capital.
Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil."
"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González said.
He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom".
An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied.
It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held.Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted.
A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election - held outside the Maduro government's official election authority - in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote.
Despite winning the primary, Maduro's government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safehouses before her fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize.
In the 2024 election, Machado's ally González ran in her place against Maduro.
The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.
The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.
Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty.
A spokesman for Machado called her return "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future".
"We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support," her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, "I don't know anything about" her return, and added that he hoped she was "safe".
"I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe," he said.
In January,Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel prize award to Trump. The committee that issues the prize had said "it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country's role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks.
"The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the US supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," he posted on X.
He added: "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy."

title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
summary: The tech billionaire accuses Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using the network for military activity.
body:
Elon Muskhas said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service,after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.
The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.
Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".
Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.
The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."
He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."
He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."
Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory.
"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram.
"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.
Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year haveprimarily been due to the Iran war.
Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.
Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.
The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
Fighting and aerial attacks continued to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.
Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.
Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.
It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.
Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with fighting now into its fifth year.

title: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation
summary: He will be observed to evaluate whether his "psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation", authorities said.
body:
A man suspected of a deadly gun attack near Paris has left custody and been placed under psychiatric observation, French anti-terrorism officials have said.
One person was killed and five others injured on Friday when an attacker opened fire from his car - first in Trappes, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin.
The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, will be observed to evaluate whether his "psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation", the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said.
President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack", adding that people had been targeted over their skin colour or religion.
It marked a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation", the French president said.
Watch: Emergency services at the scene of the shooting on Friday
PNAT said the move to place the suspect under psychiatric evaluation followed guidance from a psychiatric expert.
The evaluation will determine whether the suspect should remain in police custody and is "likely to last 48 hours", PNAT added.
PNAT said the suspect was also found to have cannabis and cocaine in his bloodstream.
French newspaper Le Monde,externaland news agency AFP report that a Bible, a Quran and a copy of Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf were found at the suspect's home, citing a source close to the investigation.
The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare".
He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately.
Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday.
The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up.
"His smile, his energy and his generosity will remain etched in our walls and in our hearts."
Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition.
The mayor of La Verrière, Nicolas Dainville, told French radio network France Info on Sunday that he had spoken to the girl's mother over the phone and confirmed she was "doing better".
Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said.
The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".
He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window.

title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
summary: Chancellor John Healey may need to raise money to boost his fiscal headroom - BBC Verify examines what options could be on the table.
body:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.
That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.
Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.
The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.
At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.
Increasingtaxes on capital gainsor extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.
BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor toraise some more money,externalon Wednesday.
Banks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money.
And there iswidespread belief among bank bossesthat the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget.
Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates,externalthat increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additional£1bn to £2bna year for the Treasury.
A higher tax would initially reduce the profits that banks have to distribute to their shareholders.
Some shareholders will be wealthy investors. The banks have warned that additional taxescould deter them from investing in the UK,external, which could reduce jobs.
And ordinary savers could be indirectly affected too, if theirpension investments include bank shares,external.
Banks could also pass some of the tax burden on to their customers by offering lower savings rates or higher borrowing costs,research suggests.,external
Former Prime MinisterGordon Brown has called on Healeyto hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.
The Social Market Foundation (SMF)think tank has estimated,externalthat doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between£275m and £460m- depending on how gamblers reacted to it.
People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.
Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.
Thegambling industry has argued,externalsuch a tax hike could cause betting shops, which own and operate the machines, to close down, by making them less profitable.
It has also argued that betting shop closures couldreduce the money bookmakers contribute to horse racing,external, potentially putting jobs in that industry at risk too.
Reports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will bemade responsible for collecting taxowed by retailers selling on their platforms.
The Treasury estimates it ismissing out on around £12bn a year,externalin VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".
Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.
Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.
Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.
Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year.
Amazon, which supports the move,has estimated it could raise£700m,externala year in VAT for the government.
Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.
However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.
The above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around £3.5bn a year.
That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits.
TheConservatives claim they could make savingsof £36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments.
Reform say they would save £50bna year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings.
Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from £68bn this year to £81bn in 2031.
Keir Starmer and Rachel Reevesattempted to reduce spending on these benefits,externalby £5bn a year by 2030, but wereforced to reverse courseafter a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.
Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.
Cuts to health and disability welfare wouldreduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments,externaland/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.
However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.

title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
summary: The move will take funding for the 10-year programme to more than £40bn.
body:
Chancellor John Healey will present his first Budget on Wednesday
More than £1bn for social and affordable housing in England will be provided in the Budget, taking funding for the government's 10-year homes programme past £40bn.
Mayors and regional leaders across England are also expected to get greater powers and funding in Wednesday's announcement - with councils helped to borrow money from the government to invest in house-building through  preferential interest rates.
It is hoped the plans will give regional leaders more flexibility and authority over investment decisions.
Chancellor John Healey said English cities and regions would get the "right to decide their own future", while Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the plans were about shifting power to those "who know their communities best".
The chancellor will also announce more support for small breweries, with the Treasury saying he wants "to turn the tide for our pint producers".
Fresh support for breweries follows the news that310 jobs are at risk at Marston's Breweryin Burton-upon-Trent.
The issue was raised again at Prime Minister's Questions earlier this week, after owners Carlsberg Britvic revealed plans to shut down operations at the historic brewing site.
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has called for Healey to resign if he fails to set out how the UK will spend 3% of the UK's GDP on defence by 2030.
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test
Under the plans for the regions, an initial £285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.
The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new £1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.
The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing High Streets back to life, or improving transport links.
Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."
Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the £285m to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".
The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."
Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.
Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.
Departing Treasury entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, has criticised the government's treatment of start-ups ahead of her last day on Thursday - the day after the Budget.
She told the Sunday Times,external, that start-ups were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy".
"Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.
Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healeyresigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan, which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.
He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.
But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".
Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.
Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

title: Will a new code end 'rip-off parking charges'?
summary: The prime minister says a new code will end "rip-off parking charges" - but will it work?
body:
Rosey Greenwood was asked to pay £1,906 because she took more than five minutes to pay for parking
"I was completely on edge, every single day," said Rosey Greenwood. "I had letters coming through - I had debt collectors after me."
Two years ago, Rosey was being told to pay £1,906 because she had taken too long to pay for parking.
Rosey had paid every single time she parked at the Copeland Street car park in Derby, and had bank records to prove it. But Rosey had unknowingly broken the car park's terms and conditions, which stipulated that drivers must pay within five minutes of entering.
Rosey could not afford to pay £1,906 - she was due to get married and also saving up to buy her first home.
As she prepared to fight the case in court, her fiance emailed the BBC and asked us to "shed some light" onwhat was happening.
The case was thenraised in Parliament,externalby Derby North MP Catherine Atkinson, who described the charges - which had caught out countless other motorists - as a "five-minute rip-off charge".
The parking sector subsequentlybanned the five-minute payment ruleby updating itscode of practice,external, but the government is going further by bringing in a statutory Private Parking Code of Practice.
"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them,"Prime Minister Andy Burnham said,externalon Monday.
But will the new code actually put the brakes on "rip-off" parking charges?
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said parking charges left people "feeling ripped off"
The government's new Private Parking Code of Practice was laid out in Parliament on Tuesday.
It sets out standards that parking operators must follow.
Housing and communities ministerFlorence Eshalomi said,externalthe new code "will give drivers a range of rights and protections to make these unfair practices a thing of the past".
The code is now subject to a 40-day period of parliamentary scrutiny, during which MPs and peers can object before it is formally issued.
The code will then come into force 21 calendar days from the point of issue.
The five-minute payment rule - as stipulated on this sign - had already been banned by the parking sector itself
In places, the code appears to be very similar to the private parking sector'sexisting code of practice,external.
For example, Eshalomi said drivers would "now have a guaranteed minimum five minutes to decide whether to park", known as the consideration period.
However, the sector's code already gives drivers a minimum consideration period of five minutes, so this does not appear to be new.
The government's code also gives drivers a10-minute grace period,externalin which to leave a car park following the end of their permitted stay.
However, the sector's code already gives drivers a 10-minute grace period, so this does not appear to be new either.
The government's code sets the maximum parking charge at £100, or £60 if paid within a fortnight. This is also the same as in the sector's code.
The government's code states chargesshould be reduced to £20 on appeal,externalunder four circumstances: not displaying a parking permit despite having a valid one, entering the wrong vehicle registration into a parking machine, not entering a registration at all, and not displaying a Blue Badge despite having one.
The sector's code already said charges should be reduced to £20 under those circumstances.
Parking operators will also still be allowed toadd a £70 debt recovery fee,externalto each parking charge if drivers do not pay, as well as court fees and legal costs.
Car park operators who break the rules should, in theory, lose access to DVLA data
The government code states parking charges should be cancelled on appeal where the driver or a passenger in the vehicle suffers the onset of illness, where the driver or a passenger is delayed by an overrunning medical appointment, where the driver suffers delays due to childcare arrangements, and where a vehicle is broken down.
In contrast, the sector's code said these charges should be reduced to £20.
The government's code says parking operators who do not comply will lose access to DVLA vehicle keeper data, meaning they will no longer be able to issue parking charges.
This is meant to happen already, because parking operators need to be members of one of two trade associations in order to access DVLA data, and they can theoretically lose their membership if they break the rules.
Campaigners claim this has not happened in practice, but the government insists it will happen in future.
There will also be what the government describes as a "fully independent Scrutiny and Oversight Board".
Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said the benefit of the new code was that it was backed by the government, rather than the parking sector itself.
"That means, if there are any changes to be made, it will come via the government and indeed via the independent scrutiny panel," he added.
"Up until now, the private industry have held the pen on changing the code of practice. Now the pen is firmly in the hand of the government."
Lynda Eagan does not believe the new code will lead to fewer parking charge notices being issued
Both the AA and RAC have welcomed the statutory code of practice - which they campaigned for - but believe it does not go far enough.
For example, the AA believes there needs to be a single and independent appeals process.
"Drivers need to have confidence that when they are making their representations, it's being heard by an independent body, as opposed to the private parking operators and their trade bodies marking their own homework," Cousens said.
The AA also believes the government needs to find an alternative to debt recovery fees and charges, which often "spiral" into the threat of court action and County Court Judgments.
This was how Rosey was asked to pay a total of £1,906 for 10 parking charges, and also howHannah Robinson was asked to pay £11,390.
The RAC shares the same concerns.
"We've long called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of parking charge notices, and a single independent appeals body to replace the two industry-run ones, but neither have been included [in the code] which is disappointing," head of policy Simon Williams said.
The government said it was "consulting as soon as possible next year on private parking debt recovery fees, including on whether to cut an existing £70 cap or scrap the fees altogether".
Parking campaigner Lynda Eagan, who helped Rosey, is sceptical about how much has changed.
"I've been screaming at the TV every time I see someone saying 'we've got these new things'," she said.
"They've tweaked a few things here and there, but it's not actually going to make an awful lot of difference to people.
"How, when not much has really changed, is that going to reduce the number of PCNs [parking charge notices]?"
In response, a Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson said: "We don't accept these claims. We've introduced a new Private Parking Code of Practice that will have statutory force and independent oversight.
"We've introduced significant changes to make life fairer for drivers, including cancelling the £20 charge for circumstances outside a someone's control like an overrunning medical appointment, and helping motorists get a fairer outcome with strengthened requirements for appeals."
One thing Eagan is looking forward to is thenew oversight board,external, although she is concerned it will not be truly independent.
The AA is more optimistic.
"We are hopeful that it could make some difference to some drivers, and we hope that it stops some of the more spurious claims being stopped at source, but we will be watching," Cousens said.
The International Parking Community said "any changes must remain fair to motorists while staying workable"
The two trade associations for parking operators, which wrote the sector's existing code, are reading and reviewing the government's changes.
Alison Tooze, chief policy officer at the British Parking Association, said: "Overall, the code strikes the right balance between stronger protections for motorists and effective parking management, helping keep communities, businesses and local economies moving."
She said retaining a £100 parking charge was important.
"Evidence shows that meaningful deterrents support compliance and good behaviours, helping ensure parking remains available for those who need it and enabling parking to be managed effectively," she added.
A spokesperson for the International Parking Community (IPC) said: "The IPC has long supported a code that raises standards, and we are now reviewing it in detail to understand what it means for motorists, landowners and operators alike.
"Any changes must remain fair to motorists while staying workable, so that compliant motorists are not disadvantaged by those who choose to ignore the rules."
Rosey married her fiance Simon, and they have bought a house together
The £1,906court claim against Rosey was droppedfollowing publicity about the case. She has since married her fiance and they have bought a house together.
She is hopeful the new code will prevent other people going through what she did.
"I feel like our voices have been heard; fellow motorists like myself have been listened to," she said.
"I hope that in the future people won't be so worried or fearful of going into car parks like the one I went to."

title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
summary: Scotland editor James Cook finds out what life is like on board a ship in an untapped oil field awaiting its fate.
body:
When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.
We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.
But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic – the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.
Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.
Nicola Boyd loves her job on the Petrojarl Rosebank vessel
This summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.
Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.
We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.
But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore.
"It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.
Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave.
"It's a job I love," she added.
The Petrojarl Rosebank is moored in the North Atlantic waiting to see if production gets the go-ahead from the UK government
It's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.
Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation – 80 miles north west of Shetland – is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.
It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.
Those conditions may be misleading.
With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge."
"Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."
Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."
Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.
Ewan Leonard says the winter weather can be "a bit of a challenge"
The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.
The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent.
"We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."
Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees.
"There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."
There's even a cinema.
Food on board the ship was described as "fantastic"
"As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.
Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.
As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.
It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.
The ship is an array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork
The ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.
If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years.
"For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge.
"We need to see this approved," he added.
Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success.
"The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.
Consent for production at Rosebank was first grantedunder the Conservative government in 2023.
But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift,the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawfulbecause they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider.
"We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation.
"If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.
Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.
It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent yearsjobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energysuch as wind and solar power.
The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.
From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.
Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.
Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.
Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura – which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor – is optimistic.
He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.
Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland – Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven.
"We would like to proceed with them," he said.
A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.
It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".
The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle
When it comes to the impending UK government decision – which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas – there is a strange mood at Rosebank.
The decision in favour of Jackdawhas clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.
For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions – no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.
And for some on board, very particular cravings.
For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board.
"My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."
It is hoped the decision on Rosebank will be made in the next few weeks
For Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery.
"I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.
But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.
She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.
For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or the another.
What are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

title: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?
summary: Voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.
body:
Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions, and being home to the rich and famous.
Now voters are about to decide whether the mega-rich among them - including media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian, and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.
Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.
There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".
What are the US midterms? A simple guide
But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades.
"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.
The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.
Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.
Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump'ssweeping tax and spending bill.
"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.
While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax,the Los Angeles Times reports,external.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.
ASeptember poll,externalfrom the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.
The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.
California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.
While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.
Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue.
In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the countryin 2022,externalthan in the preceding 13 years combined. Astudy on Switzerland,externalfound that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.
