VERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under Trump
NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox
The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.
They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.
Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax.
"I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he said, adding that the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly  given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax
Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax.
To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Metaagreed to a new stock dealthat gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.
DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".
Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who hassaid,externalhe would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believed the way the measure was written was "problematic", it was necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.
Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy.
"I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief said in an interview with the BBC's US partner CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."
Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.
While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th Century, that they have a God-given right to rule".
"They have all the wealth, they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on November 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson."
US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.
Income inequality in the US is at some of itshighest levels,externalin over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.
Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to astatewide survey,externalfrom the Public Policy Institute of California.
Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment" driving the policy.
"This is really not about Prop 40," he says, but rather about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".

title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
summary: The PM says he wants a "factual" and "evidence-based debate" about returning to free movement between Britain and Europe.
body:
Burnham says migration to the UK is "different" now compared to pre-Brexit
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.
Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said a new relationship with Brussels could include full EU membership or joining the single market, requiring free movement.
Asked about Burnham's remarks, Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg "you can't take anything off the table", adding the prime minister was saying "we've got to be pragmatic to get the best deal for Britain and he wants to have the conversation."
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch responded that the prime minister "hasn't thought this through", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick dismissed the idea as "mad".
Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.
Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
He has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, would is due by 2029.
"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," hetold the Sunday Times,external, adding he believed the type of migration had changed from revolving door movement of young people.
"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said. "The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."
But he stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."
The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.
His remarks were made ahead of an EU summit on 20 November in Brussels, where the prime minister is expected topitch options for a reset of relationswith the bloc.
On Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Rayner said she wanted to see the best possible deal with the European Union, which may well involve concessions.
"What the prime minister is saying now, and what I want, is that we have an honest conversation about the facts of what the trade-offs are to get the best deal for Britain going forward," she said.
"The frustration for me in the previous debate we had when we had the referendum is that a lot of those facts didn't get the airtime... So I would like us to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be and then put that to the people at a general election."
Writing on X, Badenoch dismissed it as "yet another example of Burnham's foot in mouth syndrome".
She added: "Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn't want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities."
Conservative MP and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, who backed Remain, warned the Brexit debate was "incredibly divisive" and insisted the current Brexit deal can still be made to work.
"I was at the top of a government that was paralysed for several years while we were trying to wrestle with the implications of that vote and I think, having made the decision, we should stick with it and make the most of it - I think we can make it a success," he told Kuenssberg.
Pointing to the one million young people not in work or training, he added: "Surely our priority in that situation is to get those jobs filled by the young people we have here instead of parking them on welfare.
"Which is why I think it's astonishing to lead on the issue of free movement... Something that is actually going to stop young people here getting jobs."
But Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper told Kuenssberg she believed allowing freedom of movement would be "a really good thing for growth" and pushed for the UK to rejoin the single market, the customs union, and also be involved in the bloc's defence pact.
The UK currently has "the worst of both worlds" on immigration, she said, as it was excluded from the EU's "new asylum pact with biometric data" that could be used to "tackle the small boats crisis".
Reform UK's economy spokesperson Robert Jenrick told Kuenssberg he had never believed freedom of movement "was a good thing", despite supporting the Remain position before the 2016 referendum when he was a Conservative MP.
"I think it's completely mad, the idea that this country needs more immigration," he said, claiming data shows mass migration "has been a disaster for working people, for Brits".
"The last thing they want is their wages being undercut by a load of low wage, low-skilled migrants from overseas," he added.

title: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
summary: Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July.
body:
The pledge was one of Burnham's key early announcements after becoming prime minister in July
Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.
Ending rough sleepingwas one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.
On the eve of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.
Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.
The BBC understands the government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas and/or they will be offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.
Some people may choose not to accept accommodation, but ministers say support will still be offered to them.
The government said initial funding had seen specialist outreach teams and new bed spaces operating in Coventry, with further provision being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden in north London over the coming weeks.
Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.
Ahead of hosting the summit, Burnham said: "Rough sleeping isn't a fact of life. It's a thing governments either choose to accept or don't.
"Well I don't accept it. That's why we're doubling funding so that people aren't just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this Parliament too.
"But we can't do it alone. If we're going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we're bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts."
More than 30 organisations have pledged support for the plan with new partnerships, including commercial businesses and charities.
Meanwhile, the National Housing Federation is working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.
However, questions remain about whether the scale of accommodation currently identified will be sufficient. It is not yet clear how many of the 2,000 homes and bedspaces represent self-contained units and how many could accommodate multiple people.
The most recent official figuresestimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough,externalon a single night in autumn 2025 in England.
While homelessness organisations have welcomed the government's focus on rough sleeping, many have urged ministers to go further in the Budget.
Leaders from 40 organisations across the housing and homelessness sector signed an open letter last week calling on the government to restore Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates so they continue to reflect local rents, arguing this would help prevent homelessness in the first place and reduce reliance on temporary accommodation.
The Resolution Foundation estimates that more than 1.1 million low income renters now face shortfalls between their housing benefit and their actual rent, with the gap expected to reach a record high this October.
It argues that relinking LHA to local rents would primarily benefit struggling tenants and help keep more people in their homes.
Housing organisations say that while helping people already sleeping rough is essential, preventing people from becoming homeless in the first place will be critical if the government's longer-term ambition is to succeed.
The Conservatives' Lam said: "Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester."
The Bed Every Night scheme Burnham set up while mayor in the region now provides more than 600 beds per night for people who might otherwise be on the streets.
He pledged to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester by 2020 when he came into power.
When he was elected in 2017 government figures showed there were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester, and by 2020 that figure had more than halved to 125 - meaning Burnham missed his target.
The numbers fell further to 90 in 2021 but the figures rose each year after that, reaching 197 by 2025.
Across England, government figures show the number ofpeople sleeping rough is at its highest levelsince records began in 2010.
Lam continued: "Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers' money and more empty promises.
"Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices.
"Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers' money."

title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents
summary: The Renters' Rights Act gives greater flexibility to leave a tenancy but the changes have posed challenges for student landlords.
body:
Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights Act
When the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.
The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.
Eddie Lever had finished his first year at the University of Exeter when he decided the course wasn't for him.
The 20-year-old wanted to switch to studying international relations at the University of York but had already organised his house for the upcoming year.
The tenancy was signed and had started.
But because of changes in the Renters' Rights Act, Eddie only had to give two months' notice before he could leave and stop paying rent.
The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months. For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.
Instead, properties are now rented on a rolling basis, which means tenants pay rent weekly or monthly with no fixed end date.
University-owned halls of residence and Purpose-Built Student Accommodation are exempt,externaland can still offer fixed-term contracts so this change primarily affects students renting from a private landlord.
"If the Renters' Rights Act wasn't a thing, I don't think I would have been able to move universities because I would have been locked into the full [year] contract," Eddie explains.
"It would have made it unaffordable."
What the Renters' Rights Act means for tenants and landlords
'I fought for change to remove student housing stress'
More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
As he was signed up to a joint tenancy, when he left it ended the tenancy for the whole house.
Fortunately, Eddie had a friend who was looking for a room who was able to take his place so his housemates could sign a new tenancy.
He acknowledges the situation would have been more difficult for his housemates if there wasn't someone who could take his room.
However, Eddie thinks the benefits for students are worth this risk.
"If you were to fall out with your flatmates or if you decide that university is not for you, being locked into a full-term contract can be really prohibitive financially," he says.
"So without that flexibility, people can really be locked into situations that they don't necessarily want to be in."
Lewis Wilson, vice president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says this flexibility means students can also save money on rent by moving home for the summer.
While previously, many student rental contracts ran into the summer after courses had finished, students can now choose to move out earlier if they want.
Wilson says students also benefit from wider changes in the act, which bans landlords in England from evicting tenants without a reason.
Campaigners argue this gives renters greater security and confidence to ask for repairs, without fearing they could be evicted if they raise concerns.
Lewis Wilson from the NUS says the legislation has given students more freedom to move out when they want
However, greater flexibility for students to leave tenancies also means less certainty for landlords.
The act did introducea specific ground,externalfor landlords to evict a group of students at the end of the academic year if they intend to re-let the property to students.
Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association, says the bigger problem for student landlords is if their tenants choose to move out earlier.
He argues this is a bigger risk for students - who may fall out with their housemates or drop out of university - than, for example, families, who are less likely to want to move out after just a few months.
Norris says the end of fixed-term tenancies means student houses could be left empty over the summer after courses finish - or even earlier.
He adds that it is now more difficult for student landlords to rent a house for just a few months as they don't know how long the tenants will stay and can't guarantee it will be available for students again in the autumn.
Norris says it's early days for the new legislation and many landlords are taking this year as a test to see how these issues play out in practice.
However, he warns that some may choose to increase the monthly rent they charge to cover the risk of their properties being empty over the summer.
In some cases, he says landlords may even sell up or stop renting to students, reducing supply and pushing up prices.
Sue Lawes thinks the changes mean many student landlords will put up their rent
Sue Lawes, who rents three shared houses to students in Norwich, is worried about the changes.
While Sue says she doesn't want to put up her prices, if her houses end up being empty over the summer because students decide to end their tenancy after their final exams she says she may have to.
She has already brought forward the start of her tenancy agreements to August instead of September to try and reduce the risks of this.
However, she says if her tenants move out earlier in the year she would struggle to make a profit, whilst covering costs including her mortgage, council tax and utility standing charges when the properties are empty.
She argues higher monthly rents would mean bigger upfront costs for students and higher overall costs for those who do choose to carry on renting over the summer.
Sue stresses that she supports the aim of the legislation to give tenants greater security and that students should be able to move out if their landlord is not carrying out repairs.
But she wants landlords to be allowed to offer fixed-term contracts to students in line with the academic year to avoid properties being left empty over the summer.
"Landlords are going to find it very, very hard to absorb those void periods," she says.
"Landlords will put prices up and students are going to pay."

title: Board of Deputies of British Jews declares Greens to be racist party
summary: The Jewish body's vote comes in response to the Green Party passing a "Zionism is racism" policy motion.
body:
The Green Party of England and Wales has been declared a racist organisation by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.
The Jewish body, which is the largest in the UK, was responding to the "Zionism is racism" policy motion passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.
Board of Deputies president Phil Rosenberg said a vote passed by 118 votes to one to declare that the Greens had, "by adopting an antisemitic platform, become a racist party".
A spokesman for the Greens insisted the party does not discriminate against people who hold Zionist views and said it rejected the Board of Deputies' "characterisation of this motion and our party".
They added the decision "will not stop us from speaking out against the genocide in Gaza and pushing for stronger sanctions against the Israeli government and its leaders". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
The motion passed by the Board of Deputies urged other parties not to do deals with the Greens unless they rejected the policy.
Forming coalition deals with Greens at local or national level would be "failing to take antisemitism with the requisite seriousness", it said, unless the party's local leadership have rejected the policy and committed to overturn it.
Labour has already issued an ultimatum to local Green groupsit is currently in coalition with, telling them to disown the motion or lose the party's support.
Rosenberg said: "By adopting an antisemitic platform, the Green Party of England and Wales has become a racist party. We will treat it accordingly.
"No political party has the right to tell Jews that a central part of our identity, rooted in thousands of years of history, faith and peoplehood, is racist.
"The Green Party's policy brands much of our community, including our synagogues and communal organisations, with that slur. It gives prejudice against Jews a political licence.
"The Green Party's leadership must now take responsibility for reversing this policy and confronting the antisemitism it has legitimised."
The motion backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, and opposition political parties.
Responding when the Green motion was passed, the Board of Deputies and Jewish Leadership Council said in a joint statement that "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".
Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote on the motion as he left the conference early to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election which was held days later.
He has since told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments,he would not overturn the motion, which would be party policy until 2028.

title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
summary: Chancellor John Healey may need to raise money to boost his fiscal headroom - BBC Verify examines what options could be on the table.
body:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.
That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.
Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.
The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.
At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.
Increasingtaxes on capital gainsor extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.
BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor toraise some more money,externalon Wednesday.
Banks in the UK have seen profits rise in recent years because they have been able to charge people higher interest rates when borrowing money.
And there iswidespread belief among bank bossesthat the chancellor is preparing to raise taxes on banks in this week's Budget.
Think tank Tax Policy Associates estimates,externalthat increasing the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax from 3% to 5.5% could potentially raise an additional£1bn to £2bna year for the Treasury.
A higher tax would initially reduce the profits that banks have to distribute to their shareholders.
Some shareholders will be wealthy investors. The banks have warned that additional taxescould deter them from investing in the UK,external, which could reduce jobs.
And ordinary savers could be indirectly affected too, if theirpension investments include bank shares,external.
Banks could also pass some of the tax burden on to their customers by offering lower savings rates or higher borrowing costs,research suggests.,external
Former Prime MinisterGordon Brown has called on Healeyto hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.
The Social Market Foundation (SMF)think tank has estimated,externalthat doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between£275m and £460m- depending on how gamblers reacted to it.
People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.
Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.
Thegambling industry has argued,externalsuch a tax hike could cause betting shops, which own and operate the machines, to close down, by making them less profitable.
It has also argued that betting shop closures couldreduce the money bookmakers contribute to horse racing,external, potentially putting jobs in that industry at risk too.
Reports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will bemade responsible for collecting taxowed by retailers selling on their platforms.
The Treasury estimates it ismissing out on around £12bn a year,externalin VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".
Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.
Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.
Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.
Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year.
Amazon, which supports the move,has estimated it could raise£700m,externala year in VAT for the government.
Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.
However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.
The above three tax measures together would raise a maximum of only around £3.5bn a year.
That would be small relative to the sums of money the chancellor might well need to restore his headroom and pay for any new spending.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in the summer he wanted a "fair and lasting" reduction to the UK's welfare bill, while the government is under pressure from opposition parties to find savings from working-age benefits.
TheConservatives claim they could make savingsof £36bn a year by restricting people's access to welfare payments.
Reform say they would save £50bna year in this way, although independent analysts say there are questions about how realistic it is to make such large savings.
Working health and sickness benefits have risen sharply since the Covid pandemic and the overall cost is projected by the Office for Budget Responsibility to increase from £68bn this year to £81bn in 2031.
Keir Starmer and Rachel Reevesattempted to reduce spending on these benefits,externalby £5bn a year by 2030, but wereforced to reverse courseafter a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.
Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.
Cuts to health and disability welfare wouldreduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments,externaland/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.
However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.
